rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: In the night journey he met Adam and prophets in successive heavens, witnessed punishments for exploiting orphans, slander, adultery, usury, and killing children, entered Paradise, saw Zayd's maiden, and negotiated the fifty prescribed prayers down to five.
rows.anchor: فوصفه النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
rows.claim: Abu Sa'id reports that after leaving Jerusalem Muhammad was carried by a beautiful ascension ladder to the guardian gate, whose keeper Isma'il commanded twelve thousand angels, each over twelve thousand.
rows.anchor: عن أبي هارون، عن أبي سعيد، قال: سمعت النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم يقول

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: The Prophet described Abraham as most resembling Muhammad; Moses as dark, tall, curly-haired and aquiline; and Jesus as ruddy, medium-height, straight-haired, with a fresh appearance like ʿUrwa ibn Masʿud.
rows.anchor: عن الزهري، عن ابن المسيب، عن أبي هريرة، أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم وصف لأصحابه

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: Anas reports that the Buraq initially balked; Gabriel asked why it resisted, since no one more honored by God had ever ridden it, and it then sweated.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة، عن أنس، أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أتي بالبراق ليلة أسري به

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says the Prophet was taken at evening from Mecca to Jerusalem, prayed there, was shown signs and given commands, then was back in Mecca by morning.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة، في قوله: {سبحان الذي أسرى بعبده ليلا من المسجد الحرام إلى المسجد الأقصى الذي باركنا حوله}

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet said the Buraq's stride reached the limit of its sight; Quraysh rejected his account of traveling to Jerusalem and returning that night, while Abu Bakr affirmed him and became al-Ṣiddīq.
rows.anchor: ذكر لنا أن نبي الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال: «حملت على دابة يقال لها البراق

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن شداد
rows.claim: At Jerusalem the Prophet chose milk over wine; Gabriel told him that he and his community had been guided.
rows.anchor: عن عبد الله بن شداد، قال: لما كان ليلة أسري برسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أتي بدابة

rows.speaker: حذيفة بن اليمان
rows.claim: An alternative report says the Prophet made the bodily journey but did not dismount, enter Jerusalem, or pray there; Hudhayfa adds that praying there would have made its prayer obligatory like prayer at the Kaaba.
rows.anchor: عن زر بن حبيش، عن حذيفة بن اليمان، أنه قال في هذه الآية: {سبحان الذي أسرى بعبده ليلا من المسجد الحرام إلى المسجد الأقصى}

rows.speaker: حذيفة بن اليمان
rows.claim: Hudhayfa insists Muhammad did not enter Jerusalem or pray there; he remained on the Buraq until he saw Paradise, Hell, and the Hereafter's prepared rewards.
rows.anchor: قال حذيفة: أجل والله الذي لا إله إلا هو ما دخله، ولو دخله لوجبت عليكم صلاة فيه

rows.speaker: معاوية بن أبي سفيان
rows.claim: Muʿawiya said that the Prophet's night journey was a true vision from God.
rows.anchor: أن معاوية بن أبي سفيان، كان إذا سئل عن مسرى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: ʿAʾisha said the Prophet's body was never absent; God took him on the journey in spirit.
rows.anchor: أن عائشة، كانت تقول: ما فقد جسد رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم، ولكن الله أسرى بروحه

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Ishaq says ʿAʾisha accepted that revelation could come to prophets awake or asleep; the Prophet's vision may have been either, but whatever he saw from God was true.
rows.anchor: قال ابن إسحاق: فلم ينكر ذلك من قولها الحسن أن هذه الآية نزلت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Tabari prefers a bodily journey: the verse says God took His servant, not merely his spirit; ordinary dreams prove no prophethood, and reports of riding Buraq and the pagans' denial require a bodily event.
rows.anchor: والصواب من القول في ذلك عندنا أن يقال: إن الله أسرى بعبده محمد

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada identifies the signs as the marvels and lessons God showed the Prophet on the way to Jerusalem.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة، قوله: {لنريه من آياتنا} [الإسراء: 1] ما أراه الله من الآيات والعبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nothing about them escapes God's knowledge; He encompasses and counts their deeds, lies in wait, and will requite each person accordingly.
rows.anchor: ولا يعزب عنه علم شيء منه، بل هو محيط بجميعه علما، ومحصيه عددا، وهو لهم بالمرصاد

rows.speaker: بعض البصريين
rows.claim: A Basran grammarian reads the initial hamza in inna as introducing Muhammad's command to say both that God made the journey and that He is Hearing and Seeing.
rows.anchor: وكان بعض البصريين يقول: كسرت «إن» من قوله: {إنه هو السميع البصير} [الإسراء: 1]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording illustrates an Arabic construction that begins an account with an absent subject then returns to direct address and related forms.
rows.anchor: من ابتداء الخبر بالخبر عن الغائب، ثم الرجوع إلى الخطاب وأشباهه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Book given to Moses is the Torah.
rows.anchor: وعنى بالكتاب الذي أوتي موسى: التوراة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Tabari says both readings are sound and compatible, but prefers the second-person form because it is more widely read.
rows.anchor: وهما قراءتان صحيحتا المعنى، متفقتان غير مختلفتين، فبأيتهما قرأ القارئ فمصيب الصواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A wakīl is a guardian or protector taken in place of God.
rows.anchor: ومعنى الكلام: وآتينا موسى الكتاب وجعلناه هدى لبني إسرائيل ألا تتخذوا حفيظا لكم سواي

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid glosses wakīl here as a partner, since treating something besides God as His substitute makes it a partner.
rows.anchor: عن ابن أبي نجيح، عن مجاهد، في قوله: {ألا تتخذوا من دوني وكيلا} [الإسراء: 2] قال: شريكا

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says the Book was guidance that brought the Israelites from darkness to light and was mercy for them.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة، قوله: {وآتينا موسى الكتاب وجعلناه هدى لبني إسرائيل} [الإسراء: 2] جعله الله لهم هدى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address concerns all peoples addressed by the Quran, Arabs and non-Arabs, Israelites and others, because every human on earth descends from Noah's rescued passengers.
rows.anchor: وعنى بالذرية: جميع من احتج عليه جل ثناؤه بهذا القرآن من أجناس الأمم

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says all people descend from those saved in the Ark: Noah, three sons, his wife, and three women; Shem fathered Arabs, Ham Ethiopians, and Japheth Romans.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة، {ذرية من حملنا مع نوح} [الإسراء: 3] والناس كلهم ذرية من أنجى الله في تلك السفينة

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: A report through Maʿmar from Qatada names Noah, his wife, their three sons, and the sons' wives as the survivors.
rows.anchor: عن معمر، عن قتادة: {ذرية من حملنا مع نوح} [الإسراء: 3] قال: بنوه ثلاثة ونساؤهم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid likewise names Noah, his three sons and their wives as the survivors, but says Noah's wife was not among them.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: بنوه ونساؤهم ونوح، ولم تكن امرأته

rows.speaker: سلمان
rows.claim: Salman says Noah was called grateful because he praised God whenever he put on clothes or ate.
rows.anchor: عن أبي عثمان، عن سلمان، قال: كان نوح إذا لبس، ثوبا أو أكل طعاما حمد الله

rows.speaker: سعيد بن مسعود
rows.claim: Saeed ibn Masʿud similarly says Noah never wore a new garment or ate without praising God.
rows.anchor: عن أبي حصين، عن عبد الله بن سنان، عن سعيد بن مسعود، بمثله

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says Noah praised God for new and worn clothes and after drinking, thanking Him for a satisfying, pleasant, healthy drink; al-Tabari notes this reached him as a report, not as interpretation.
rows.anchor: عن مجاهد، {ذرية من حملنا مع نوح} [الإسراء: 3] من بني إسرائيل وغيرهم

rows.speaker: عمران بن سليم
rows.claim: ʿImran ibn Sulaym says Noah thanked God for food, drink, clothing, shoes, and relief after relieving himself, recognizing that God could have withheld each benefit.
rows.anchor: عن النضر بن شفي، عن عمران بن سليم، قال: إنما سمي نوح عبدا شكورا

rows.speaker: ابن أبي مريم
rows.claim: Ibn Abi Maryam says Noah praised God after defecating for making it easy, removing its harm, and preserving its usefulness.
rows.anchor: أن ابن أبي مريم، حدثه قال: إنما سمى الله نوحا عبدا شكورا

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says Noah praised God whenever he got or wore a garment and urged anyone receiving new clothes to praise God for clothing and covering him.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة، قال الله لنوح {إنه كان عبدا شكورا} [الإسراء: 3] ذكر لنا أنه لم يستجد ثوبا قط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here al-Tabari takes qadaynā as informing Israel through Moses and the revealed Book that they would corrupt the land twice and become greatly arrogant.
rows.anchor: موسى صلوات الله وسلامه عليه بإعلامه إياهم، وإخباره لهم

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd glosses qadaynā ilayhim as 'We informed them.'
rows.anchor: قال ابن زيد، في قول الله: {وقضينا إلى بني إسرائيل} [الإسراء: 4] قال: أعلمناهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas also glosses the phrase as 'We informed them.'
rows.anchor: عن علي، عن ابن عباس، في قوله: {وقضينا إلى بني إسرائيل} [الإسراء: 4] يقول: أعلمناهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another report from Ibn ʿAbbas takes it as a decree against Israel in the primordial record and God's prior knowledge.
rows.anchor: عن أبيه، عن ابن عباس، {وقضينا إلى بني إسرائيل} [الإسراء: 4] قال: هو قضاء قضي عليهم

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada likewise understands the phrase as a decree God imposed on the people.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة، قوله: {وقضينا إلى بني إسرائيل} [الإسراء: 4] قضاء قضاه على القوم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid also glosses the phrase as God's informing the Israelites.
rows.anchor: عن مجاهد، في قوله: {وقضينا إلى بني إسرائيل في الكتاب} [الإسراء: 4] قال: أخبرنا بني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Tabari prefers 'informed them': the readers agree on addressing Israel with the t-form of 'you will corrupt'; a decree imposed on them would more naturally take the y-form.
rows.anchor: وإن كان الذي اخترنا من التأويل فيه أشبه بالصواب لإجماع القراء على قراءة قوله {لتفسدن} [الإسراء: 4] بالتاء دون الياء

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says Israel's first corruption was killing Zechariah; a Nabataean king sent Persian troops, but the campaign initially withdrew after Nebuchadnezzar, disguised as a beggar, overheard Israel's fear, until Israel later attacked and recovered its property.
rows.anchor: عن السدي، في خبر ذكره عن أبي صالح، وعن أبي مالك، عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd identifies the two corruptions as killing Zechariah and his son John: Sapor of Persia was sent for Zechariah's killing, and Nebuchadnezzar for John's.
rows.anchor: قال ابن زيد: كان إفسادهم الذي يفسدون في الأرض مرتين: قتل زكريا ويحيى بن زكريا

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report from Hudhayfa says Nebuchadnezzar devastated Jerusalem over Zechariah's blood, killing seventy thousand, enslaving Israel and taking its treasures to Babylon; after a century Cyrus restored the survivors and Temple treasure, but Israel sinned again and another Persian assault came.
rows.anchor: عن ربعي بن حراش، قال: سمعت حذيفة بن اليمان، يقول: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Hudhayfa's report continues: a Roman king later captured Israel and burned Jerusalem; the Prophet says the Mahdi will return the Temple treasure, carried in a great fleet to Jaffa, where God will gather the first and last generations.
rows.anchor: فقال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: «هذا من صنعة حلي بيت المقدس

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Ishaq relates that Moses had foretold Israel's two corruptions and that God had long shown mercy despite their sins; kings were paired with prophetic advisers who upheld Torah rather than bringing new scriptures.
rows.anchor: قال: كان مما أنزل الله على موسى في خبره عن بني إسرائيل، وفي إحداثهم ما هم فاعلون بعده

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: In Ibn Ishaq's account, after King Ṣiddīqiyyā's reign Israel's sins grew, Sennacherib invaded with six hundred thousand standards, and Isaiah warned the sick king; God then granted his prayer fifteen more years and saved Jerusalem.
rows.anchor: بعث الله عليهم سنحاريب ملك بابل، ومعه ست مائة ألف راية

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Al-Tabari takes Israel's arrogance as presumption against God and defiance of His command, while Mujahid instead says they would exalt themselves over other people.
rows.anchor: عن مجاهد، {ولتعلن علوا كبيرا} [الإسراء: 4] قال: ولتعلن الناس علوا كبيرا

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says the first promise is the first of the two occasions of corruption decreed for Israel.
rows.anchor: قال ابن زيد، في قوله: {فإذا جاء وعد أولاهما} [الإسراء: 5] قال: إذا جاء وعد أولى تينك المرتين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas glosses jāsū as 'they walked.'
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس، {فجاسوا خلال الديار} [الإسراء: 5] قال: مشوا

rows.speaker: بعض أهل المعرفة بكلام العرب من أهل البصرة
rows.claim: A Basran Arabic authority says jāsū means 'they killed,' citing Hassan's verse; al-Tabari allows both senses, since the troops could kill while roaming the houses.
rows.anchor: وكان بعض أهل المعرفة بكلام العرب من أهل البصرة يقول: معنى جاسوا: قتلوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Tabari says either lexical sense works: the troops could kill the inhabitants as they moved through the homes.
rows.anchor: وجائز أن يكون معناه: فجاسوا خلال الديار فقتلوهم ذاهبين وجائين، فيصح التأويلان جميعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their movement through the houses was a promise God certainly fulfilled, for He does not break His promise.
rows.anchor: وكان جوس القوم الذين نبعث عليهم خلال ديارهم وعدا من الله لهم مفعولا ذلك لا محالة لأنه لا يخلف الميعاد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: One report names Goliath as the first attacker; he imposed tribute and humiliation until Saul was appointed, David killed Goliath, and Israel regained its kingdom.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس، قوله: {فإذا جاء وعد أولاهما بعثنا عليكم عبادا لنا أولي بأس شديد

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada likewise names Goliath of al-Jazira as the first attacker, who captured and killed people while roaming Israel's homes.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة، قوله: {فإذا جاء وعد أولاهما بعثنا عليكم عبادا لنا أولي بأس شديد

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says God first gave Goliath power over Israel until David, serving with Saul, killed him.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة، قال: أما المرة الأولى فسلط الله عليهم جالوت، حتى بعث طالوت ومعه داود

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Another view names Sennacherib of Assyria and Nineveh. Saʿid ibn Jubayr tells of an Israelite who prayed to see Israel's destroyer, found the Babylonian orphan Nebuchadnezzar, cared for him, and secured his promise of obedience if he ever ruled.
rows.anchor: عن ابن جريج، قال: ثني يعلى بن مسلم عن سعيد بن جبير، أنه سمعه يقول: كان رجل من بني إسرائيل يقرأ

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: In Saʿid ibn Jubayr's account, Nebuchadnezzar was chosen to lead four thousand cavalry to Syria, captured people without killing or destroying, returned as king, and had learned Syria's vulnerabilities by talking with its people.
rows.anchor: الذي ذكر سعيد بن جبير أنه قال لهم

rows.speaker: سعيد بن المسيب
rows.claim: Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib says Nebuchadnezzar destroyed Jerusalem and Israel, then killed seventy thousand people in Damascus over a blood that bubbled on a rubbish heap until it stopped.
rows.anchor: عن يحيى بن سعيد، قال: سمعت سعيد بن المسيب، يقول

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Another view identifies the attackers as people of Persia and says there was no battle in the first episode.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون: يعني بذلك قوما من أهل فارس، قالوا: ولم يكن في المرة الأولى قتال

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid's account identifies the attackers as a Persian intelligence detachment accompanying Nebuchadnezzar; they gathered information, left without fighting, and Israel later won.
rows.anchor: عن ابن أبي نجيح، عن مجاهد، {فإذا جاء وعد أولاهما بعثنا عليكم عبادا لنا أولي بأس شديد فجاسوا خلال الديار}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Tabari says God returned the advantage to Israel over the people sent against them; traditions describe either an Israelite raid reclaiming property, the enemy king's peaceful release of captives and goods, or victory over Goliath.
rows.anchor: ثم أدلناكم يا بني إسرائيل على هؤلاء القوم الذين وصفهم جل ثناؤه أنه يبعثهم عليهم

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says the Israelites became more numerous in David's time.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة، قوله {وجعلناكم أكثر نفيرا} [الإسراء: 6] أي عددا، وذلك في زمن داود

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi glosses 'more numerous' as greater in number.
rows.anchor: عن السدي، {وجعلناكم أكثر نفيرا} [الإسراء: 6] يقول: عددا

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says God restored Israel's advantage after its defeat and then increased its numbers.
rows.anchor: قال ابن زيد، في قوله: {ثم رددنا لكم الكرة عليهم} [الإسراء: 6] لبني إسرائيل، بعد أن كانت الهزيمة

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says the advantage was restored to the Israelites.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة، {ثم رددنا لكم الكرة عليهم} [الإسراء: 6] ثم رددت الكرة لبني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: سفيان
rows.claim: Sufyan says their supply of money and sons numbered four thousand.
rows.anchor: عن سفيان، في قوله: {وأمددناكم بأموال وبنين} [الإسراء: 6] قال: أربعة آلاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Doing good by obeying God and keeping His commands benefits Israel itself: in this world He repels enemies and increases wealth and strength, and in the next He grants Paradise; disobedience angers God, empowers enemies, and earns humiliating punishment.
rows.anchor: يا بني إسرائيل، فأطعتم الله وأصلحتم أمركم ولزمتم أمره ونهيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase fa-lahā means fa-ilayhā, 'against/for it,' as in 99:5, where awḥā lahā means awḥā ilayhā.
rows.anchor: {وإن أسأتم فلها} [الإسراء: 7] والمعنى: فإليها كما قال {بأن ربك أوحى لها}

rows.speaker: قراء أهل المدينة والبصرة
rows.claim: Medina and Basra readers use plural li-yasūʾū, making the dispatched attackers the subject; the parallel 'and that they enter' supports this reading.
rows.anchor: والبصرة {ليسوءوا وجوهكم} بمعنى: ليسوء العباد

rows.speaker: قراء الكوفة
rows.claim: Kufa readers use singular li-yasū; it can mean the day of the promise makes faces ugly, with 'came' elided, or that God makes them ugly, with 'we sent them' elided.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ذلك عامة قراء الكوفة: (ليسوء وجوهكم) على التوحيد وبالياء

rows.speaker: بعض أهل العربية من الكوفيين
rows.claim: Some Kufa grammarians read la-nasūʾa in the first-person plural, as God's own statement about making their faces ugly.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ذلك بعض أهل العربية من الكوفيين: «لنسوء وجوهكم» على وجه الخبر من الله

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi recounts an Israelite dream that Babylonian orphan Nebuchadnezzar would destroy Israel; the Israelite befriended him and secured safe-conduct, while John's refusal to approve the king's desired marriage led to the Baptist's beheading and blood that boiled up to the city walls.
rows.anchor: عن السدي، في الحديث الذي ذكرنا إسناده قيل: إن رجلا من بني إسرائيل رأى في النوم

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: The narrative says Nebuchadnezzar led the campaign; an old Israelite woman showed him how prayer over John's blood would make the city collapse, then urged him to kill seventy thousand people until the blood stopped.
rows.anchor: فقالت له: إنه بلغني أنك تريد أن ترجع بجندك قبل أن تفتح هذه المدينة

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Nebuchadnezzar spared the bearer of his safe-conduct, sacked Jerusalem, defiled the Temple, exiled Israel's leaders and Daniel with other prophetic descendants, and took them to Babylon.
rows.anchor: وخرب بيت المقدس، وأمر به أن تطرح فيه الجيف، وقال: من طرح فيه جيفة

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: At Babylon, Daniel and his companions were falsely accused of rejecting the king's god; after being thrown into a pit with a fierce lion, they survived unharmed alongside a seventh figure who appeared among them.
rows.anchor: فأمر بخد فخد لهم، فألقوا فيه وهم ستة، وألقى معهم سبعا ضاريا

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: The seventh figure was an angel who struck Nebuchadnezzar and turned him into a wild creature for seven years; God later restored his kingship, and Daniel survived both the lions' pit and a fiery furnace.
rows.anchor: فخرج إليهم السابع، وكان ملكا من الملائكة، فلطمه لطمة

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Daniel interprets Nebuchadnezzar's dream of a multi-metal statue: successive empires would be Babylon, Persia, fragmented kingdoms, then an Arab prophet would destroy their remaining power as a stone shattered the statue.
rows.anchor: أما الصنم الذي رأيت رأسه من ذهب، فإنه ملك حسن مثل الذهب

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: The Magi exploited Nebuchadnezzar's inability to remember his dream and tried to kill Daniel; later they framed Daniel over drinking and urination, but God withheld his urine and the king was accidentally killed by his own guard.
rows.anchor: فحبس الله عن دانيال البول، وكان أول من قام من القوم يريد البول بختنصر

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿid ibn Jubayr says the first attacker was Sennacherib, but after Israel sinned again Nebuchadnezzar came a second time, killed the fighters, enslaved families, took wealth, entered and defiled Jerusalem; God then restored Israel and warned that renewed sin would bring renewed punishment.
rows.anchor: عن أبي المعلى، قال: سمعت سعيد بن جبير، قال: بعث الله عليهم في المرة الأولى سنحاريب

rows.speaker: أبو المعلى
rows.claim: Abu al-Muʿalla says he knows of the promise to restore Israel's kingdom only from this report, and the report itself does not promise that return.
rows.anchor: فقال أبو المعلى، ولا أعلم ذلك، إلا من هذا الحديث، ولم يعدهم الرجعة إلى ملكهم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says the second destruction came when the Persian king of Babylon sent Nebuchadnezzar against Israel; he devastated them, fulfilling the later promise.
rows.anchor: عن مجاهد، {فإذا جاء وعد الآخرة ليسوءوا وجوهكم} قال: بعث الله ملك فارس ببابل
